practiceSet.title: U5.LT1 Practice: Identifying Forces
practiceSet.description: Practice naming the forces on an object, telling mass from weight, and calculating weight with W = m × g.

activity.title: U5.LT1 Relearning: Identifying Forces
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can identify forces acting on an object.

**Think of a backpack on your shoulder.** You feel it pulling down on you (that's gravity), and you feel your shoulder strap holding it up. Every object is like that backpack: something is always pulling or pushing on it, even when it is sitting still. Your job is to name each push or pull and say which way it points.

**A force is a push or a pull.** Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**. One newton is the force needed to give a 1-kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^{2} (1 N = 1 kg·m/s^{2}).

**The named forces.** **Gravity (Fg)** is a long-range pull toward Earth; it points **down**. **Normal force (FN)** is the support force from a surface; it is always **perpendicular** to the surface (up from a floor or table). **Applied force (Fapp)** is a push or pull a person or object puts on, like pulling a wagon. **Friction (Ff)** is the force between two surfaces; it opposes motion, so it points **opposite** the direction of motion. **Air resistance (Fair)** is friction from air; it also points opposite the motion (up on a falling object). **Tension (T)** is the force from a string, rope, or cable; it pulls along the rope (up for something hanging).

**Types of friction.** **Static** friction: the surfaces are not moving (a desk that won't budge). **Sliding** friction: one surface slides across another (a box pushed across the floor). **Rolling** friction: a wheel or ball rolls (bike tires on the road).

**Mass vs. weight.** **Mass** is the amount of matter, in kg. **Weight** is the force of gravity on an object, in N. Mass does not change in outer space, but weight does, because g changes. **W = m × g**, with g = 9.8 m/s^{2} on Earth (Moon 1.6, Mars 3.7, Jupiter 24.8 m/s^{2}). To find mass, rearrange: **m = W ÷ g**.

**Worked example 1:** What is the weight of a 72 kg student on Earth? Formula: W = m × g. Set up: W = 72 kg × 9.8 m/s^{2}. Answer: **705.6 N**.

**Worked example 2:** A dresser weighs 539 N on Earth. What is its mass? Formula: m = W ÷ g. Set up: m = 539 N ÷ 9.8 m/s^{2}. Answer: **55 kg**. On the Moon its mass is still 55 kg.

**Worked example 3:** A 185 kg rover lands on Mars (g = 3.7 m/s^{2}). Which forces act on it while it sits still on level ground, and what is its weight there? Forces: Fg down and FN up (nothing pushing it sideways, so no applied force or friction). Formula: W = m × g. Set up: W = 185 kg × 3.7 m/s^{2}. Answer: **684.5 N**.

**Watch out for:** dividing when you should multiply (weight is always a bigger number than mass on Earth), swapping mass and weight or their units (kg vs. N), using 9.8 on another planet, adding a "force of the kick" or "force of motion" after the push has stopped, and pointing friction the same way the object moves.
prompts: A wagon is pulled to the right across a sidewalk with a rope. List every force acting on the wagon and the direction each one points.
Explain the difference between mass and weight, and tell what happens to each when an astronaut goes from Earth to Mars.
Calculate the weight of a 64 kg student on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s^{2}). Show the Formula, Set up, and Answer with units.
Name the type of friction (static, sliding, or rolling) for: a parked bike that won't move when you nudge it, a sled sliding down a snowy path, and a rolling basketball. Explain each choice.
